justice: Street space is dominated by a wide carriageway, while there is no clearly built sidewalk on either side, indicating an uneven allocation of space between motorized and non-motorized users.
Cyclists, a scooter rider, and a three-wheeler are all using the same travel space as cars, suggesting limited modal separation and only moderate fairness for different road users.
The road edges appear unpaved or grassy in several places, and no curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked accessible pedestrian paths are visible, reducing universal accessibility.
safety: The road is relatively straight with long forward visibility, which helps users detect approaching vehicles earlier.
There are no visible marked crosswalks, traffic-calming devices, or protected shoulders, so pedestrians and cyclists would face conflicts when moving along or across the road.
Mixed traffic is evident: a bicycle, scooter, three-wheeler, parked car, and motor vehicle lane all share close proximity, increasing interaction risk.
Utility poles and overhead wires line the roadside, but no clearly visible pedestrian refuge, guardrail, or separated facility is present.
livability: The corridor has substantial roadside greenery and mature trees, which improves environmental quality and visual relief.
However, the street lacks visible shops, benches, bus stops, or active public-frontage uses, so it offers limited support for daily social life and street vitality.
Large fenced plots and setback buildings on the left create a low-activity edge, reducing opportunities for casual interaction and surveillance.
sustainability: A bicycle rider and small two-/three-wheeled vehicles are present, indicating that the street is being used by lower-carbon transport modes.
Dense roadside vegetation and large trees contribute to shading, ecological value, and some air-quality benefits.
Despite the greenery, there is no visible dedicated bike lane, transit stop, or stormwater infrastructure such as bioswales or permeable drainage features.
The broad paved carriageway still prioritizes vehicle movement, which limits the overall sustainability performance.
aesthetics: The large tree canopy on the right and continuous green vegetation along the corridor create a pleasant natural edge.
Open sky views and distant mountains provide strong visual depth and a scenic backdrop.
The street appears relatively clean and uncluttered, with low sign clutter and simple roadside composition.
At the same time, the utilitarian fencing, exposed wires, and plain road surface reduce design refinement.
comfort: The mature tree on the right casts substantial shade onto part of the roadway and edge, improving thermal comfort locally.
Shade coverage is uneven, with the left side and much of the carriageway exposed to direct sun, so heat comfort would be limited in hot weather.
There are no visible benches, shelters, or formal resting spaces, reducing physical comfort for people spending time outside the street.
Low building density and a relatively open corridor likely reduce crowding stress, but the absence of a clear pedestrian zone lowers psychological comfort for walkers.
walkability: No continuous paved sidewalk is clearly visible on either side; instead, road edges transition into dirt, grass, or narrow informal margins.
There are no marked pedestrian crossings, curb extensions, or pedestrian-priority features to support safe walking trips.
The long block form and sparse frontage activity make the route less engaging and less supportive for everyday walking.
Tree shade on the right improves the walking environment somewhat, but it does not compensate for the lack of dedicated pedestrian infrastructure.
bikeability: A cyclist is visible using the roadside space, showing that cycling is possible on this corridor.
The road appears fairly wide and straight, which can provide basic riding space and good forward sightlines.
However, there is no marked or protected bike lane, so cyclists must share space with scooters, three-wheelers, and cars.
The road edge condition is inconsistent, with narrow shoulders and some rough or unpaved margins, which reduces cycling comfort and security.
